# Syllabus - Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless

## Module overview

This module builds the skills of a modern cloud engineer: provisioning and operating **cloud infrastructure as code** with a proper **DevOps / GitFlow** practice, and designing **serverless, event-driven applications** on top of it.

Working in teams of three, you will bootstrap **a production-grade cloud project** on the

provider of your choice (**GCP** or **AWS**), deploy a foundation **infrastructure** (network, IAM,

managed **Kubernetes** cluster with self-hosted **CI/CD** runners) entirely with **Terraform** and

**Helm**, then build a fully **serverless and event-driven**, **real-time** collaborative drawing platform (a

Reddit r/place style pixel canvas) driven by a Discord bot and **a reactive web frontend**.

Everything, from the foundation to the last **serverless** function, is deployed through

**Infrastructure as Code** and automated **CI/CD** pipelines, and observed through a **monitoring**

and **alerting** stack.

## Target audience and level

Final-year engineering students who already have general software development experience.

No prior cloud, Terraform, Kubernetes, or serverless experience is strictly required, but a minimum network knowledge is expected.

## Cloud provider prerequisites

You choose **one** provider (**GCP** or **AWS**) for your hands-on work and final project. The supports cover both. All requirements have an equivalent implementation on each provider; choose based on your team's familiarity.

**Note that it's** **required to claim free credits on your cloud provider**.

Details and step-by-step setup are in **C01 - Prerequisites & Project Bootstrap**.

## Pedagogical objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- **Operate on a public cloud provider** (GCP or AWS): navigate its core managed services, understand the serverless and cloud-native model, and keep resource usage and costs under control across separate development and production environments.
- **Apply DevOps and GitFlow principles** in a real team setting: feature branches, pull requests, code review, immutable releases, and automated delivery through CI/CD pipelines with GitHub Actions, using keyless authentication to the cloud (OIDC / Workload Identity Federation).
- **Author production-grade Infrastructure as Code** with Terraform and Helm: multi-environment, remote state, modules, variables, and least-privilege IAM.
- **Deploy and scale a managed Kubernetes cluster** (GKE / EKS) hosting self-hosted GitHub Actions runners that scale horizontally through node autoscaling.
- **Design and implement a secure, event-driven serverless architecture** on the cloud: API Gateway, functions following the Single Responsibility Principle, message brokers, serverless storage, and NoSQL data modeling for a very large or near-infinite canvas, integrating a Discord bot through Discord Interactions with request signature validation.
- **Build a reactive, real-time web frontend** that updates without polling and stays performant on a large grid of pixels.
- **Secure the whole system**: manage secrets and identities across GitHub, applications, cloud secret manager, and Kubernetes, and apply least privilege everywhere.
- **Instrument, monitor, trace, and alert** on both the cluster and the serverless workloads, and demonstrate scalability under load.
- **Present and defend** an architecture and its implementation, justifying design choices.

# Subject - Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless

## Foreword

You will design, build, document, and defend a **production-grade cloud-native platform** on a single public cloud provider of your choice (GCP or AWS). The platform has two layers:

- A **foundation** deployed entirely as Infrastructure as Code: network, IAM, a managed Kubernetes cluster, and self-hosted GitHub Actions runners that scale horizontally.
- A **serverless, event-driven application**: a collaborative real-time pixel canvas (inspired by Reddit's r/place) driven by a Discord bot and a reactive web frontend, also deployed entirely as Infrastructure as Code through CI/CD pipelines.

Everything is glued together by a proper **DevOps / GitFlow** practice, secured with least-privilege IAM, proper secrets management, following the single responsibility principle (SRP) and observed through a **monitoring, tracing, and alerting** stack.

With this subject comes **9 documents** named **C00** to **C08**, it will serve as support during your in-class courses but are mainly **aimed to help you** achieve this project **successfully**.

They contain **theoretical courses**, **hands-on**, **examples**, **diagrams**, **checklists about your deliverables, useful takeaways** and also **describe technical expectations** about the whole project. You should follow them **during the whole duration** of your project, reading them, using them as reference and official guidelines for this module, alongside this subject.

## 00\. Introduction

Modern cloud engineers do not choose between "infrastructure" and "application". They own both, expressed as code, delivered through automated pipelines, and operated with observability. This module makes you practice that reality end to end.

You will acquire and demonstrate the following skills:

- **DevOps** and **GitFlow** collaboration in a team.
- **Infrastructure as Code** with **Terraform** and **Helm** across two environments.
- **CI/CD** with **GitHub Actions** and keyless cloud authentication (OIDC / Workload Identity).
- Operating a managed **Kubernetes cluster** hosting autoscaling self-hosted **runners**.
- Designing and building a **secure**, **scalable**, **event-driven** **serverless** application.
- Integrating a **Discord** bot and a real-time web **frontend**.
- **Monitoring**, **tracing**, **alerting**, and proving **scalability** under load.

## 01\. Prerequisites

Complete all of the following before building anything.

### 1.1 Team

- Form a **group of 3 students**. All members work on the **same repository** and the **same cloud projects/accounts**.
- **Lock your group on the Epitech Intranet.**

### 1.2 Repository and commit signing

- Create a **new private Git repository**, hosted on Github but not on the Epitech GitHub organization (you will need features not available there).
- Each student creates a **personal GPG key** and configures their git CLI to **sign commits and tags** with it. All commits must be signed and shown as _Verified_.
- Grant repository access (through IaC where possible) to all team members and to me [Kloox](https://github.com/Kloox).

### 1.3 Cloud accounts

- Create an account on your chosen provider (GCP or AWS), **claim free-tier credits**, and configure **billing**.
- Provision **two isolated environments**: one dev and one prd (two GCP projects, or two AWS accounts). Naming example: teamX-cloudnative-dev and teamX-cloudnative-prd.
- Grant the instructor access to both environments so resources and billing can be reviewed:
  - GCP: add <jeremie@jjaouen.com> as Editor.
  - AWS: create an IAM user with proper permissions and share credentials securely to me.

## 02\. Foundation

This chapter covers the **DevOps**/**GitFlow** structure of your repository, the deployment of your **Kubernetes** cluster and your custom runners for **GitHub**.

Everything here is deployed with **Terraform and Helm**, driven by **CI/CD pipelines**,

and split cleanly across the dev and prd environments.

### 2.1 Scope

Deploy, as code, the following on your chosen provider:

- **Networking**: VPC, subnets, NAT / egress, and the routing required by your cluster.
- **IAM**: users, roles, service accounts, and bindings, following **least privilege**.
- Human access (team + instructor) should be managed in a **separate Terraform stack** so that destroying the workload does not revoke people's access.
- **Managed Kubernetes cluster** (GKE or EKS), with at least one node pool dedicated to the CI/CD runners.
- **Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners** deployed **inside the cluster with Helm**. Runners must **scale horizontally through node autoscaling** (not only pod scaling).
- **OIDC / Workload Identity Federation** so that GitHub Actions authenticates to the cloud with **short-lived credentials**, scoped to your repository and environment. No long-lived cloud keys stored in GitHub.
- **Secrets management**: proper use of the cloud **secret manager**, **GitHub secrets/environments**, and **Kubernetes secrets**, with no secret ever committed to the repo.

### 2.2 DevOps / GitFlow and CI/CD requirements

- Implement a **GitFlow** that reflects DevOps values: short-lived feature branches, pull requests with review, an immutable main, and versioned releases (for example v1.2.0 tags) that trigger deployments.
- Your pipeline(s) must at least:
  - Validate Terraform: terraform fmt -check and terraform validate.
  - Run terraform plan for both dev and prd.
  - On release (tag), **apply** to dev then prd, using the GitHub Actions **environment** feature.
  - Provide **manual destroy** workflows for dev and prd.
- Once the runners exist, route appropriate jobs to your **self-hosted runners** and manage a proper way to switch between GitHub provided runners and yours (labels, inputs, or dispatch).
- Keep infrastructure **reproducible** (apply) and **disposable** (destroy): after a destroy, no billable resource should remain except the human-access stack.

### 2.3 Cost and safety

Autoscaling misconfiguration can burn your free credits quickly. Set budgets/alerts, size your nodes sensibly, and put safeguards on runner scaling.

**References:**

- **C02 - Infrastructure as Code with Terraform**
- **C03 - GitFlow & CI/CD Pipelines**
- **C04 - Managed Kubernetes, Helm & Self-Hosted Runners**

## 03\. Serverless

Build a **fully serverless** collaborative pixel canvas. Every serverless component must be deployed with **Infrastructure as Code** and delivered through **CI/CD pipelines** with the same GitFlow discipline as the foundation.

The reference for the kind of shared canvas you are building is Reddit's r/place:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### 3.1 Mandatory architectural constraints

- **100% serverless**: no VMs, no Kubernetes workloads, no manually managed servers for the application. (The cluster hosts only your CI/CD runners, not the app.)
- **All public entry points go through an API Gateway** (or provider equivalent). Functions must **not** be invokable directly over the internet, bypassing the gateway.
- **Event-driven and asynchronous**: all real work flows through a **message broker** (Pub/Sub, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, or EventArc). Public-facing functions are lightweight proxies that authenticate the request, acknowledge quickly, and publish an event.
- **Single Responsibility Principle**: each function does one clear thing.
- **Serverless persistence only**: serverless NoSQL (Firestore / DynamoDB) and object storage (Cloud Storage / S3). No self-managed or SQL database.
- **Least privilege**: a dedicated service account / IAM role per function or service.
- **Secrets** in the secret manager; **HTTPS** end to end.

### 3.2 Discord bot

Build a **serverless** Discord bot using **Discord Interactions** (slash commands) with the interaction endpoint pointing at **your API Gateway**. Using a persistent gateway SDK such as discord.js or discord.py in a long-running process is **off subject**: it is not serverless.

You must validate the **Discord request signature** (Ed25519) in your proxy before doing anything else, and respond to the PING handshake.

The commands are **predefined and mandatory**. Implement exactly these:

<div class="joplin-table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th><p><strong>Command</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Parameters</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Behavior</strong></p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/draw</code></pre></th><th><p>x (int), y (int), color (hex or palette value)</p></th><th><p>Draw a single pixel at (x, y) with color. Subject to per-user rate limiting. Acknowledge immediately, process asynchronously.</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/get</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Return the <strong>current state</strong> of the grid as a PNG or JPEG image (the visible/rendered canvas).</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/snapshot</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Generate a <strong>timestamped</strong> PNG/JPEG of the current grid, store it in a bucket (S3 / GCS), and return a <strong>pre-authenticated (signed) URL</strong> to the Discord channel.</p></th></tr><tr><th><p>/admin pause and /admin resume</p></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Pause or resume drawing globally. While paused, /draw and web draws are rejected. Admin only.</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/admin clear</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Clear the entire grid. Admin only.</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/admin ratelimit</code></pre></th><th><p>user (Discord user), limit (int per minute)</p></th><th><p>Set a per-user rate limit override. Admin only.</p></th></tr></thead></table></div>

**Notes:**

- Admin commands must be **authorized** (Discord role or an allow-list you control); a normal user must not be able to run them.
- Every command must go through: **API Gateway -> proxy function -> queue -> worker**. The proxy acknowledges (Discord deferred response is acceptable); the worker performs the action and, where relevant, edits the response or posts a follow-up.

### 3.3 Data model and the large grid

- The grid must be **at least 10000x10000 pixels**, or effectively **infinite**, and remain **performant** for reads, writes, and rendering. Design your data model accordingly (chunking, tiling, delta encoding, and caching are expected considerations; storing the full grid as one document is not acceptable at this size).
- For every pixel in the current state, record at least the **color**, the **author**, and the **update timestamp**. A user must be able to inspect a pixel and see who set it and when on the frontend.
- Enforce **per-user rate limiting** (a sensible default, for example 20 pixels/minute, overridable by the /admin ratelimit command).
- Maintain **consistency under concurrent updates**.

### 3.4 Web frontend

- The frontend must be **serverless** (any serverless hosting/tech of your choice: static hosting + CDN, Cloud Run, App Engine, CloudFront + Lambda@Edge, a Discord Activity, etc.).
- Users authenticate with **Discord OAuth2** (or custom identities linked to their Discord account). Keep scopes minimal; do not persist user access tokens server-side.
- The canvas view must update in **real time through events / streaming**. **Polling and manual refresh buttons are not allowed.** The displayed state must be the up-to-date state at any moment.
- The frontend must stay **performant on the full 10000x10000 (or infinite) grid** (viewport rendering, zoom/pan, chunked loading, only transmit changed pixels, etc.).
- A user must be able to **select a pixel** to see its author and update timestamp, and to draw on it.
- Provide a **brush tool** that draws **multiple pixels at once**, with a **configurable brush size**.
- All API calls from the frontend must be **authenticated** and pass through the same gateway + event pipeline (no direct writes to storage).

**References:**

- **C05 - Serverless Foundations**
- **C06 - Event-Driven Serverless Architecture & Data Design**
- **C07 - Discord Bot, Real-Time Frontend & Snapshots**.

## 04\. Monitoring and Observability

You choose the tools; you must meet the requirements. Suggested options include Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, and the native cloud services (Cloud Monitoring / Cloud Logging / Cloud Trace, or CloudWatch / X-Ray). Justify your choices at the defense.

You must be able to:

- See the **metrics** and state of your cluster: CPU, RAM, node count, pod count, and the activity of your self-hosted runners.
- See the **metrics** and state of your serverless application: invocations, errors, latency, queue depth / message age, and DLQ counts.
- Integrate application **logs** and **traces** into your monitoring solution and be able to search and analyze them. A single request must be traceable end to end using a **correlation ID** (or similar) propagated across services.
- Set up **alerts** for critical issues (high error rate, high latency, queue backlog, resource saturation, and similar).

You must be able to demonstrate scalability during the defense: show, through your monitoring, that the system scales and stays performant under load (runner node scaling for the foundation, serverless scaling and queue buffering for the application). A load test (custom script or a tool such as Locust) is one way; the brush drawing many pixels at once can also generate the load. What matters is proving it with proper monitoring.

**Reference:**

- **C08 - Monitoring, Logging, Tracing & Alerting**.

## 05\. Defense

The defense is where you prove understanding, not just delivery. Every member must be able to explain the whole system.

### 5.1 Defense conditions

The defense is held **remotely on** Microsoft Teams , at the slot scheduled on the Epitech intranet. Connect on time; the slot will not be extended for setup problems.

Before the defense, every member must have checked that they **all** have and can use:

- A **decent** microphone.
- A webcam (preferably).
- A **stable** internet connection.
- The ability to **share their screen** during the defense.

These are individual prerequisites: each student must be able to speak, and present from their own machine. If any of these conditions is not met, the student may have his defense invalidated.

### 5.2 What to prepare

- The **production environment** is the reference. It must be live and reachable.
- A maintained, **provider-specific** architecture diagram that matches reality (foundation and serverless, flows, protocols, IAM boundaries, queues, and workers).
- Your **repository**: GitFlow history, pull requests, signed commits, CI/CD runs and all deliverables.
- A way to **demonstrate scaling** under load (a load test as Locust, the brush generating load, or similar), observed through your monitoring.

### 5.3 What you will be asked to demonstrate

- The full flow from your IDE to production (edit, PR, review, release, deploy).
- Your custom runners are up and used in your GitHub repository.
- The serverless app is up, functional, using a real-time refresh and use a large-grid.
- Scaling: runner node scaling and serverless/event scaling, shown on your dashboards.
- Security: least-privilege IAM, non-public functions/buckets, secret management, HTTPS, OIDC / Workload Identity, and signature validation for Discord.
- Monitoring, logs, traces, and at least one meaningful alert.

### 5.4 Use of open source

You may use community GitHub Actions, Helm charts, Terraform modules/providers, and libraries, provided that:

- You can **justify why** you use them.
- You can **explain what they do**.
- They do **not** introduce security issues, and they are reasonably maintained/adopted.

### 5.5 External help and AI

You are free to build your project however you want, including with AI assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude and similar), code generators, tutorials, or help from others. There is no restriction on the tools you use to get there.

The rule is simple: whatever you use, you must be able to **explain and demonstrate every part** of your project during the defense, the infrastructure as well as the code. If you cannot explain a part of your work, it counts as if it were not yours, regardless of how it was produced. AI is a tool to help you learn and build faster, not a replacement for understanding what you deliver.

**NOTE**: Using AI assistance during the oral defense **IS NOT** acceptable and would be flagged as **cheating**.

### 5.6 Evaluation

Your project can be graded **FAILED** or with a **letter grade from D to A**, with an increasing level of expectation: **D** certifies the minimum base expected in a company (a functional, serverless, event-driven application deployed as Infrastructure as Code through a working CI/CD pipeline, with essential security, a diagram that matches reality, and a team able to explain it), while **C, B, and A** require progressively more completeness, correctness, security, observability, demonstrated scalability, and defense quality.

Evaluation covers the areas described throughout this subject:

- Team collaboration, workflow, and the quality of your oral defense.
- Repository and GitFlow: branching, signed commits, pull requests, CI/CD, secrets.
- Foundation: network, IAM, cluster, and self-hosted runners deployed as code, with keyless authentication (OIDC / Workload Identity).
- Serverless application: serverless and event-driven compliance, the mandatory Discord commands, the real-time frontend, the data model, and deployment as code through CI/CD.
- Security: least privilege, secret management, securing access.
- Observability: monitoring, logging, tracing, alerting, and demonstrated scalability.
- Architecture diagram and internal documentation.

A project **cannot pass** if it has no architecture diagram, or no functional application that can be demonstrated, or if the team cannot explain their infrastructure, work, and application. Every point is assessed against your live production environment, your repository, and your oral defense.

### 5.6. Deliverables checklist

- **Group locked on the Intranet, private repo, GPG-signed commits.**
- **Two environments (dev, prd) on your provider, instructor granted read access.**
- **Foundation (network, IAM, cluster, runners) deployed by Terraform + Helm via CI/CD.**
- **OIDC / Workload Identity in place; no long-lived cloud keys in GitHub.**
- **Runners scale via node autoscaling.**
- **Serverless app deployed by IaC via CI/CD: API Gateway, proxies, queues, workers, NoSQL, buckets.**
- **Discord bot with all mandatory commands, signature validation, async processing.**
- **Real-time serverless frontend, brush tool, large-grid performance, Discord OAuth2.**
- **Monitoring, logging, tracing, alerting for cluster and app; scaling demonstrable.**
- **Maintained provider-specific architecture diagram and internal documentation.**

# C00 - Introduction: Cloud, DevOps & Serverless Fundamentals

## 1\. Why this module exists

Modern cloud engineers own an entire vertical slice: the network, the identities, the delivery pipelines, and the application, all expressed as code and operated with observability. This module makes you practice that reality by merging two disciplines that are usually taught separately:

- Infrastructure as Code and DevOps: building and delivering cloud infrastructure the same way you build software.
- Serverless: designing event-driven applications that scale automatically without you managing servers.

You will build a foundation (network, IAM, a managed Kubernetes cluster hosting your CI/CD runners) and, on top of the same DevOps practice, a fully serverless collaborative drawing platform. Everything is Infrastructure as Code, everything ships through pipelines.

## 2\. What is the cloud?

Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of computing resources (compute, storage, databases, networking, and higher-level managed services) over the internet, billed by usage. Instead of buying and operating hardware, you rent capabilities from a provider. The two providers covered in this module are **Google Cloud Platform (GCP)** and **Amazon Web Services (AWS)**. You pick one for your project; the concepts transfer.

### 2.1 Service models

- **IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)**: you rent compute, storage, and network; you manage the OS and everything above. Example: Compute Engine, EC2.
- **PaaS (Platform as a Service)**: the provider manages the runtime; you deploy code. Example: App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk.
- **SaaS (Software as a Service)**: fully managed software consumed through a browser. Example: Gmail, Salesforce.
- **FaaS (Function as a Service)**: you deploy individual functions that run only when triggered and scale per request. This is the heart of **serverless**. Example: Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, AWS Lambda.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### 2.2 Deployment scope

Providers expose resources at different scopes:

- **Global**: spanning regions (for example a global load balancer or IAM).
- **Regional**: within one region made of multiple isolated data centers (for example us-central1, eu-west-1).
- **Zonal**: within a single availability zone.

Choosing a region has real consequences on **cost**, **latency**, and **environmental impact**. Choose deliberately.

### 2.3 Provider services

##

| Category             | AWS                   | GCP                              |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Serverless functions | Lambda                | Cloud Functions, Cloud Run       |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| Object storage       | S3                    | Cloud Storage                    |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| Serverless NoSQL     | DynamoDB              | Firestore                        |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| Messaging            | SQS, SNS, EventBridge | Pub/Sub, EventArc                |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| API gateway          | API Gateway           | API Gateway                      |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| Managed Kubernetes   | EKS                   | GKE                              |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| Secrets              | Secret Manager        | Secret Manager                   |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| Monitoring / logging | CloudWatch, X-Ray     | Cloud Monitoring, Logging, Trace |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |
| Identity             | IAM                   | IAM                              |
| ---                  | ---                   | ---                              |

Both providers use a **shared-responsibility model**: they secure the underlying infrastructure, you secure your workloads and configuration.

## 3\. Why automate infrastructure?

Managing cloud resources by clicking in a console feels fast at first and becomes a liability:

- **Human error**: misconfigurations, accidental deletions.
- **Inconsistency**: dev and prd drift apart, the classic "it works on my machine".
- **No history**: nobody knows who changed what and when.
- **Poor scaling of effort**: manual steps do not keep up with real workloads.

Automating with Infrastructure as Code (IaC) brings:

- **Reproducibility**: recreate an environment identically with one command.
- **Idempotence**: applying the same config repeatedly converges to the same state and corrects drift.
- **Versioning**: the infrastructure lives in Git, reviewed and revertible.
- **Speed and reliability**: fewer manual steps, fewer mistakes.

You will use Terraform (cloud-agnostic, declarative) and Helm (Kubernetes package manager) as your IaC tools. See C02 and C04.

## 4\. DevOps and GitOps in one paragraph

**DevOps** is a culture and a set of practices that shorten the loop between writing code and running it in production reliably: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, and back again.

GitOps applies DevOps to infrastructure and applications by using Git as the single source of truth: whatever is declared and merged in Git is what gets deployed, automatically, by pipelines. Your **GitFlow** (branching, pull requests, reviews, releases) is therefore as important as your Terraform code.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## 5\. What is serverless?

Serverless does not mean "no servers"; it means you do not manage them. The provider handles provisioning, scaling, availability, and patching. You focus on code and data.

### 5.1 Characteristics

- **Event-triggered**: functions run in response to HTTP calls, messages, storage changes, or schedules.
- **Automatic scaling**: from zero to many instances, per request.
- **Pay-per-use**: billed by invocation and duration.
- **Stateless**: no in-memory persistence between invocations; state lives in external storage.

### 5.2 Benefits and trade-offs

**Benefits:** No infrastructure to manage, elastic scaling, cost efficiency at variable load, tight integration with cloud IAM/logging.

**Trade-offs to design around:**

- **Cold starts**: a small delay when a function spins up after inactivity.
- **Execution limits**: maximum runtime and memory per invocation.
- **Stateless design**: you must externalize state.
- **Distributed debugging**: harder to reproduce locally; observability matters more.

### 5.3 When serverless fits

Event-driven systems, APIs with irregular traffic, scheduled jobs, lightweight automation, and real-time data pipelines. It fits the pixel-canvas project perfectly: bursts of draw events, asynchronous processing, and elastic fan-out.

## 6\. The big picture of your project

Everything you build in this module comes together in a single project. Before diving into the technical supports, here is a tour of the parts you will assemble and how they relate.

### 6.1 The provider and the two environments

You pick one cloud provider (GCP or AWS) and run everything on it. The whole project is duplicated across two isolated environments, dev and prd, so you can iterate safely and promote changes only once they are proven. The same code produces both; nothing is created by hand in a console.

### 6.2 The foundation

The foundation is the base infrastructure that everything else sits on: a private network, identity and access management (IAM), and a managed Kubernetes cluster (GKE or EKS). The cluster has one job in this project: hosting your self-hosted GitHub Actions runners, which scale with demand through node autoscaling. It does not host the application. The foundation is written as Infrastructure as Code with Terraform and Helm.

### 6.3 The delivery pipeline

Nothing is deployed from a laptop. GitHub Actions is your delivery mechanism: it runs your

tests and terraform plan on pull requests, and applies changes to dev and then prd on

release. Pipelines authenticate to the provider with keyless auth (OIDC / Workload Identity),

so no long-lived cloud credentials ever live in GitHub. Your GitFlow discipline (branches,

reviews, tags) is what drives these deployments.

### 6.4 The serverless application

The application itself is a fully serverless, event-driven collaborative pixel canvas, in the spirit of Reddit's r/place. Its main components are:

- **Entry point:** an API Gateway that receives every public request.
- **Proxies:** thin functions behind the gateway that validate each request and hand the real work off asynchronously.
- **Broker:** a queue or topic that decouples the entry point from the processing.
- **Workers:** functions that consume events, apply the business rules, and update the data stores.
- **Data:** a serverless NoSQL database holding the grid state, and object storage holding snapshots.
- **Frontend:** a reactive web app that renders the shared canvas.

### 6.5 Observability

The last component spans everything above: a monitoring stack with metrics, logs, traces,

and alerts, covering both the cluster and runners (foundation) and the serverless

application. It is how you prove the system works, scales, and behaves correctly, and how

you debug it when it does not.

###

## 7\. Key takeaways

- The cloud delivers resources as a service; you choose GCP or AWS for this module.
- IaC (Terraform, Helm) makes infrastructure reproducible, idempotent, and versioned.
- DevOps/GitOps make Git the source of truth and pipelines the delivery mechanism.
- Serverless abstracts servers away and fits event-driven, bursty workloads.
- Your project combines a foundation (IaC + cluster + runners) with a serverless app, delivered and observed as one system.
