# C02 - Infrastructure as Code with Terraform

_Reference material for the module_ **_Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless_**_. This support teaches Terraform from principles to a working, remote-state deployment. It ends with_ **_Hands-on 1_**_: deploy a VPC and a subnet on your provider._

## 1\. Why Terraform

Terraform is a widely used, cloud-agnostic, declarative IaC tool. You describe the desired state in HCL, Terraform figures out the difference with reality and converges to it. Since version 1.0 it guarantees backward compatibility, and its provider ecosystem covers AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, Helm, and much more. Three principles underpin everything:

- **Reproducibility**: the same configuration yields the same infrastructure, every time, in every environment.
- **Idempotence**: applying repeatedly converges to the same state and corrects drift (changes made manually in the console get detected and reverted on the next apply).
- **Versioning**: the configuration lives in Git, reviewed through pull requests and revertible.

## 2\. How Terraform works

- **Providers** talk to a platform's API (aws, google, kubernetes, helm) and expose **resources**.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

- **State** is Terraform's memory: a file mapping your code to real resources. It enables planning, drift detection, and collaboration when stored remotely.
- **Plan** computes what will change (create / update / destroy).
- **Apply** executes the plan through the provider APIs.

write code (desired) -> terraform plan (diff) -> terraform apply (converge) -> state updated

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## 3\. Anatomy of a configuration

### 3.1 Providers

# providers.tf

```
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.9"
  required_providers {
    aws    = { source = "hashicorp/aws",    version = "~> 6.0" }
    google = { source = "hashicorp/google", version = "~> 7.0" }
  }
}
# choose the one you use
provider "aws" {
  region = var.region
}
provider "google" {
  project = var.project_id
  region  = var.region
}
```

### 3.2 Variables

Parameterize everything that differs between environments. Never hardcode project ids, regions, or CIDRs.

# variables.tf

```
variable "project_id" {
  type        = string
  description = "Cloud project id (GCP) or account alias (AWS)"
}
variable "region" {
  type        = string
  description = "Region for resources"
}
variable "vpc_name" {
  type        = string
  description = "Name of the VPC"
}
variable "cidr_block" {
  type        = string
  description = "CIDR block for the VPC"
}
```

Mark anything sensitive:

variable "some_secret" {

```
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
```

### 3.3 Resources and outputs

# main.tf (AWS example)

```
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block = var.cidr_block
  tags       = { Name = var.vpc_name }
}
resource "aws_subnet" "main" {
  vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block = "10.0.1.0/24"
  tags       = { Name = "${var.vpc_name}-subnet" }
}
output "vpc_id" {
  value       = aws_vpc.main.id
  description = "The id of the created VPC"
}
```

GCP equivalent:

resource "google_compute_network" "main" {

```
  name                    = var.vpc_name
  auto_create_subnetworks = false
}
resource "google_compute_subnetwork" "main" {
  name          = "${var.vpc_name}-subnet"
  network       = google_compute_network.main.id
  ip_cidr_range = "10.0.1.0/24"
  region        = var.region
}
output "vpc_id" {
  value       = google_compute_network.main.id
  description = "The id of the created VPC network"
}
```

Every resource's arguments and attributes are documented in the **Terraform Registry**. That registry is your reference; get used to reading it.

## 4\. Dependencies

Terraform builds a dependency graph from references between resources. If a subnet references a VPC id, Terraform creates the VPC first. Use depends_on only when Terraform cannot infer the order automatically.

## 5\. Remote state (required)

Local state is unsafe for teamwork. You must use a **remote backend** (a bucket) so the state is shared and locked.

- The backend bucket must exist **before** terraform init. Create it once (manually or with a small script), then bring it under Terraform control with terraform import.
- A backend block **cannot** use variables, so keep the backend config in per-environment files.

AWS S3 backend:

# backend.tf

```
terraform {
  backend "s3" {}
}
```



# backends/dev.hcl

```
bucket = "teamX-dev-tfstate"
key    = "foundation/terraform.tfstate"
region = "eu-west-1"
```



terraform init -backend-config=backends/dev.hcl

GCP GCS backend:

terraform {

```
  backend "gcs" {}
}
```



# backends/dev.hcl

```
bucket = "teamX-dev-tfstate"
prefix = "foundation"
```



terraform init -backend-config=backends/dev.hcl

State locking (.tflock) is created automatically during plan/apply and prevents concurrent operations against the same state.

## 6\. The core workflow

terraform init -backend-config=backends/dev.hcl

```
terraform fmt -check
terraform validate
terraform plan -var-file=dev.tfvars
terraform apply -var-file=dev.tfvars
# ... and to tear down:
terraform destroy -var-file=dev.tfvars
```

Your infrastructure must be:

- **Reproducible**: one command to create (apply).
- **Disposable**: one command to remove (destroy), leaving nothing billable behind (except the separate human-access stack, see C03).

The same code, applied with a different -var-file, produces identical infrastructure in each environment:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## 7\. Security and good practices

- Use variables for region, project, and CIDRs; never hardcode secrets.
- Mark secrets sensitive = true; store real secret values in a secret manager, not in tfvars.
- Authenticate locally through the CLI; in CI/CD use OIDC / Workload Identity (C03).
- Prefer official/community modules when they are well maintained, and understand what they do before using them.
- Avoid null_resource and local-exec except as a genuine last resort.

## 8\. Hands-on 1: deploy a VPC and a subnet

**Goal**: a reproducible, disposable VPC + subnet with remote state, on your provider, in dev.

1. **Create the state bucket** for dev (script or console), then plan to import it later.
2. Write providers.tf, variables.tf, main.tf, backend.tf, dev.tfvars, and backends/dev.hcl. dev.tfvars example:

project_id = "teamX-cloudnative-dev"

```
region = "us-central1" # or your AWS region
vpc_name = "teamX-dev-vpc"
cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
```

1. Run the workflow:

terraform init -backend-config=backends/dev.hcl

```
terraform fmt -check && terraform validate
terraform plan -var-file=dev.tfvars
terraform apply -var-file=dev.tfvars
```

1. Confirm the VPC and subnet exist in the console, and read the vpc_id output.
2. Tear it down and confirm nothing remains:

terraform destroy -var-file=dev.tfvars

1. Commit your code. Do **not** commit state or credentials.

**Acceptance**: apply creates exactly the VPC + subnet with remote state; destroy removes them; re-running apply recreates them identically without manual steps.

**Go further**: add a prd.tfvars with a different region and CIDR, and a separate backends/prd.hcl, so the same code deploys both environments. This is the bridge to C03.

## 9\. Key takeaways

- Terraform converges reality to a declared desired state; think reproducibility, idempotence, versioning.
- Providers expose resources; state is memory; plan diffs; apply converges.
- Remote state is mandatory for teamwork; backend config cannot use variables.
- Parameterize per environment; keep secrets out of code.
- You can now create and destroy a network stack with one command each.

# C03 - GitFlow & CI/CD Pipelines

_Reference material for the module_ **_Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless_**_. This support turns your local Terraform into an automated, multi-environment delivery pipeline with keyless cloud authentication. It ends with_ **_Hands-on 2_**_: a pipeline that deploys your Terraform stack through a proper GitFlow._

## 1\. Why GitFlow matters as much as your code

Your branching strategy defines how your team collaborates and how safely you ship. A good GitFlow embodies DevOps values:

- **Fast to fail**: test early, short feedback loops (validate and plan on every PR).
- **Immutability**: do not mutate infrastructure by hand; change code and redeploy.
- **Time to market**: keep merges and releases lightweight.
- **Collaboration**: feature branches, pull requests, and reviews.
- **The DevOps cycle**: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor.

You are free to design your own GitFlow, but it must make sense against these values. Look at established models before committing to one, and think carefully about which jobs run in which branch, context, and environment.

## 2\. A workable branching model

A simple, effective model for this project:

- **main**: always deployable, protected, requires PR + review + green checks.
- **feature/\***: short-lived branches for one change.
- **Pull requests**: run fmt, validate, and plan for both environments; nothing is applied yet.
- **Releases** are tags (v1.2.0, semantic versioning). Tagging triggers deployment: apply to dev, then prd.

**Note that signed commits (C01) are expected across the history.**

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

## 3\. GitHub Actions basics

Workflows live in .github/workflows/\*.yml and react to events (push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch, tags). Key building blocks you will use:

- **Matrix** to run the same job for dev and prd.
- **Environments** (environment: prd) to scope secrets and add protection/approval.
- **Permissions** including id-token: write for OIDC.
- **Reusable/community actions**, provided they are well maintained, understood, and safe.

## 4\. Keyless cloud authentication: OIDC / Workload Identity Federation

Never store long-lived cloud credentials in GitHub. Instead, GitHub Actions presents a short-lived **OIDC token**; the cloud validates it and issues **temporary credentials** scoped to the job.

**Security rule**: the cloud must issue credentials **only** when the token proves it comes from **your repository** and the **correct environment** (dev/prd). This prevents another repo or another environment from assuming your identity.

### 4.1 GCP (Workload Identity Federation)

- Create a **Workload Identity Pool** and a **provider** trusting GitHub&apos;s OIDC issuer.
- Bind a **service account** to identities matching your repo and branch/environment via an attribute condition (for example assertion.repository == &apos;your-org/your-repo&apos;).
- In the workflow, authenticate with google-github-actions/auth using the pool provider and service account (no key file).

### 4.2 AWS (OIDC role assumption)

- Create an **IAM OIDC identity provider** for token.actions.githubusercontent.com.
- Create an **IAM role** with a trust policy conditioned on sub/aud matching your repo and environment.
- In the workflow, use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume and id-token: write (no access keys).

Because Workload Identity/OIDC setup is provider-specific and evolves, follow the official GitHub and provider documentation.

## 5\. CI/CD pipeline requirements (from the subject)

Your pipeline must:

- Validate Terraform: terraform fmt -check and terraform validate.
- Run terraform plan for both dev and prd.
- On release (tag), **apply** to dev then prd, using GitHub Actions **environments**.
- Provide **manual destroy** workflows for dev and prd.
- Use variables for anything environment-specific.
- Contain **no** secrets/credentials hardcoded or committed.

Later, once the cluster and runners exist (C04), route your pipelines jobs to your **self-hosted runners** and manage a proper way to switch runners (labels, inputs, or dispatch).

## 6\. Example: CI on pull requests

# .github/workflows/terraform-ci.yml

```
name: Terraform CI
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write # required for OIDC
jobs:
  validate-plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        env: [dev, prd]
    environment: ${{ matrix.env }}
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/foundation
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      # Authenticate with OIDC (GCP example; swap for AWS as needed)
      - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: ${{ vars.WIF_PROVIDER }}
          service_account: ${{ vars.DEPLOYER_SA }}
      - run: terraform fmt -check
      - run: terraform init -backend-config=backends/${{ matrix.env }}.hcl
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -var-file=${{ matrix.env }}.tfvars
```

## 7. Example: deploy on release

# .github/workflows/terraform-deploy.yml

```
name: Terraform Deploy
on:
  push:
    tags: [&apos;v*&apos;]
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      max-parallel: 1 # dev must succeed before prd
      matrix:
        env: [dev, prd]
    environment: ${{ matrix.env }} # add required reviewers on prd
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/foundation
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: ${{ vars.WIF_PROVIDER }}
          service_account: ${{ vars.DEPLOYER_SA }}
      - run: terraform init -backend-config=backends/${{ matrix.env }}.hcl
      - run: terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=${{ matrix.env }}.tfvars
```

## 8. Example: manual destroy

# .github/workflows/terraform-destroy.yml

```
name: Terraform Destroy
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      env:
        description: "Environment to destroy (dev or prd)"
        required: true
        default: dev
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
jobs:
  destroy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ github.event.inputs.env }}
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/foundation
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: ${{ vars.WIF_PROVIDER }}
          service_account: ${{ vars.DEPLOYER_SA }}
      - run: terraform init -backend-config=backends/${{ github.event.inputs.env }}.hcl
      - run: terraform destroy -auto-approve -var-file=${{ github.event.inputs.env }}.tfvars
```

These examples are intentionally minimal. Extend them (linting, security scans, cost estimation, tests, notifications) and adapt them to your GitFlow.

## 9\. IAM and human access as a separate stack

Manage the permissions of team members and me (on the cloud and on the Git host) in a **separate Terraform stack**. A destroy of the foundation or app must not lock people out.

Example (GCP):

resource "google_project_iam_member" "instructor_viewer" {

```
  project = var.project_id
  role    = "roles/editor"
  member  = "user:jeremie@jjaouen.com"
}
```

## 10. Managing secrets across the stack

- **GitHub**: repository/environment secrets and variables for pipeline configuration.
- **Cloud secret manager**: runtime secrets (Discord tokens, API keys), accessed by workloads through IAM.
- **Kubernetes secrets**: for in-cluster needs.

Nothing sensitive is ever committed. Use sensitive = true in Terraform and reference the secret manager rather than inlining values.

## 11\. Hands-on 2: deploy your Terraform stack through the pipeline

**Goal**: your VPC + subnet from Hands-on 1 (C02) is now deployed by CI/CD, not by hand, with OIDC and a real GitFlow.

1. Set up OIDC / Workload Identity for your repo and both environments (no cloud keys in GitHub). Store the provider id and deployer service account/role as GitHub **variables**.
2. Add the three workflows above (CI, deploy, destroy), pointing at infra/foundation.
3. Protect main: require PR, review, and passing checks. Add required reviewers on the prd environment.
4. Open a feature/\* branch, add a change (for example a second subnet), open a **PR**, and confirm the CI runs fmt, validate, and plan for dev and prd.
5. Merge, then create a **tag** v0.1.0. Confirm the deploy workflow applies to dev then prd using OIDC.
6. Trigger the **destroy** workflow for dev and confirm resources are removed.

**Acceptance**: a signed-commit PR shows plans for both envs; a release tag deploys to both envs through OIDC with no stored cloud key; destroy works from the pipeline; main is protected.

## 12\. Key takeaways

- GitFlow is a first-class deliverable: feature branches, PRs, reviews, immutable releases.
- Pipelines validate and plan on PRs, apply on release, and can destroy on demand.
- Use OIDC / Workload Identity for keyless, scoped cloud authentication.
- Keep human access in a separate stack; keep every secret out of the repo.
- You can now ship infrastructure changes entirely through automation.

# C04 - Managed Kubernetes, Helm & Self-Hosted Runners

_Reference material for the module_ **_Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless_**_. This support covers the managed cluster that hosts your CI/CD runners: Kubernetes core concepts, managed-cluster specifics, Helm, deploying self-hosted GitHub Actions runners, node autoscaling, and secrets. In this module the cluster exists_ **_only_** _to run your self-hosted runners; there is no application workload on it._

## 1\. Kubernetes core concepts

### 1.1 Cluster, nodes, control plane

- A **cluster** is a set of machines (**nodes**) managed together.
- **Nodes** are the workers where pods run.
- The **control plane** manages cluster state: the API server (entry point), the scheduler (places pods), the controller managers (reconcile desired vs actual), and etcd (state store).![](data:image/png;base64,)

### 1.2 Workloads

- **Pod**: one or more containers sharing network and storage; ephemeral.
- **ReplicaSet**: keeps N identical pods running.
- **Deployment**: manages ReplicaSets for stateless apps; supports rolling updates and rollbacks. This is what runner charts typically use.
- **DaemonSet**: one pod per node (monitoring agents, node exporters).
- **StatefulSet**: stable identities and storage for stateful apps.
- **Job / CronJob**: run to completion / on a schedule.

Cross-cutting ideas: **spec vs status** (desired vs observed, continuously reconciled), **labels and selectors** (how controllers find pods), and **immutability** (pods are replaced, not mutated).

### 1.3 Services and networking

Pods get ephemeral IPs; **Services** give a stable endpoint:

- **ClusterIP**: internal only.
- **NodePort**: exposes a node port.
- **LoadBalancer**: provisions a cloud load balancer (managed clusters).
- **Headless**: direct DNS records.

CoreDNS provides service discovery; **NetworkPolicies** restrict pod-to-prop traffic.

### 1.4 Scaling

- **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)**: scales pod count on CPU/memory/custom metrics.
- **Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)**: adjusts requests/limits.
- **Cluster / Node Pool Autoscaler**: adds/removes nodes when pods cannot be scheduled.

For runners, **node autoscaling is the key lever**: as more jobs demand more runner pods, the node pool must grow, then shrink when idle.

### 1.5 Namespaces and RBAC

Namespaces isolate logically (for example a dedicated runners namespace). RBAC grants fine-grained permissions to users and service accounts; in managed clusters it works together with cloud IAM.

## 2\. Managed cluster specifics (GKE / EKS)

- **Managed control plane**: the provider runs and patches the API server, etcd, and controllers. You do not manage them.
- **Node pools**: groups of identically configured nodes. Use a dedicated pool for runners so you can autoscale and size it independently. Each pool has its own machine type, taints, and labels.
- **Hybrid identity**: access depends on **cloud IAM** (can you reach the cluster?) plus **Kubernetes RBAC** (what can you do inside?).
- **Networking**: the cluster integrates with your VPC; nodes/pods draw IPs from your subnets; NAT handles egress for private nodes.
- **Upgrades**: control plane upgrades are managed; schedule node pool upgrades and maintenance windows.

## 3\. Helm

Helm is the required tool for deploying the runners. It is a package manager for Kubernetes; packages are **charts** that bundle templated manifests, configured through values.yaml.

### 3.1 Using charts

helm repo add &lt;name&gt; &lt;url&gt;

```
helm repo update
helm install <release> <name>/<chart> --values values.yaml --namespace runners --create-namespace
```

Prefer **official or well-maintained community charts**; understand what they deploy.

### 3.2 values.yaml

values.yaml overrides defaults without editing templates (replica count, image, resources, autoscaling). Parameterize per environment.

### 3.3 Terraform + Helm

Manage Helm releases as code with the helm_release resource so the cluster and its workloads stay in one IaC flow:

resource "helm_release" "runners" {

```
 name = "gha-runners"
 repository = "https://<chart-repo>"
 chart = "<runner-chart>"
 version = "x.y.z"
 namespace = "runners"
 create_namespace = true
 values = [file("values/runners-${var.environment}.yaml")]
}
```

Benefits: consistency with the rest of your IaC, versioned releases, deployment through CI/CD.

## 4\. Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners

### 4.1 Why

GitHub-hosted minutes are limited. Self-hosted runners let you offload CI/CD jobs to your cluster and are a required part of this module.

### 4.2 Requirements

- Deploy runners **with Helm** (official or well-maintained community chart, for example the Actions Runner Controller ecosystem).
- Runners **register dynamically** with your repository and **unregister** after jobs.
- Runners **scale horizontally through node autoscaling**: pod demand drives node pool growth and shrink.
- Authenticate the controller to GitHub securely (GitHub App or token stored as a secret, never committed).

### 4.3 Routing jobs and switching runners

Target self-hosted runners with labels:

jobs:

```
 heavy:
  runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, terraform]
```

Avoid committing a workflow change every time you switch between GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners. Use dynamic labels, environment variables, or workflow_dispatch inputs:

jobs:

```
 deploy:
  runs-on: [self-hosted, "${{ inputs.runner_label }}"]
```

Once your runners are deployed, ensure that all your jobs runs on it when available.

### 4.4 Cost safety

Autoscaling misconfiguration can consume free credits quickly. Choose modest machine types, cap the maximum node count, set idle scale-down, and put budget alerts in place. Log runner activity and clean up stale registrations.

## 5\. Secrets management in and around the cluster

- **Cloud secret manager**: source of truth for runtime secrets; workloads read via IAM.
- **Kubernetes secrets**: for in-cluster consumption (consider integrating them from the cloud secret manager rather than hand-creating them).
- **GitHub secrets/environments**: pipeline configuration and the runner controller&apos;s GitHub credential.
- Never commit secrets. Apply least privilege to every service account and RBAC binding.

## 6\. Putting it together (foundation recap)

By the end of the foundation you should have, all as code and delivered by CI/CD:

VPC + subnets (C02)

```
 |
IAM: least-privilege SAs/roles, human access in a separate stack (C03)
 |
GKE/EKS cluster with a dedicated runner node pool (this support)
 |
Helm-deployed self-hosted GitHub runners, node-autoscaling (this support)
 |
OIDC/WIF so pipelines authenticate without stored keys (C03)
```

## 7. Checklist

- Cluster deployed with Terraform, with a dedicated runner node pool.
- Runners deployed with Helm (via helm_release), registering dynamically.
- A CI job actually runs on a self-hosted runner.
- Node autoscaling demonstrably adds/removes nodes under runner load.
- There is no secret/credentials exposed (commited in repo, not using keyless auth for runners, etc)
- Max node count and budget alerts configured to protect credits.
- Commits are signed.

## 8\. Key takeaways

- Kubernetes reconciles desired state through controllers; Services and DNS provide stable networking over ephemeral pods.
- Managed clusters hand you the control plane; node pools and hybrid IAM/RBAC are your levers.
- Helm (through Terraform) deploys your runners as versioned, reproducible releases.
- Self-hosted runners must register dynamically and scale through node autoscaling, with strict cost safeguards.
- The cluster in this module serves the runners only; the application is serverless.

# C05 - Serverless Foundations: Functions, IAM & API Gateway

_Reference material for the module_ **_Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless_**_. This support introduces the building blocks of the serverless application: functions, securing them with IAM, and exposing them safely through an API Gateway. Everything here will be deployed as Infrastructure as Code (see C06)._

## 1\. Serverless functions

Functions are the core compute unit of serverless. They:

- run only when **triggered** (HTTP request, message, storage change, schedule),
- **scale automatically** with demand, from zero to many,
- **billed per invocation and duration**,
- **stateless**; state lives in external storage.

Provider options you will use:

- **GCP**: **Cloud Functions** (event-driven) or **Cloud Run** (containerized services with more flexibility). Both are serverless when configured to scale on demand.
- **AWS**: **Lambda**, integrating natively with S3, SQS, EventBridge, API Gateway, and more.

Design each function around the **Single Responsibility Principle**: one function, one clear job (a proxy, a draw worker, a snapshot generator, a notifier, etc.). This keeps IAM tight, testing simple, and scaling predictable.

## 2\. Securing access with IAM

IAM controls who and what can invoke or manage your resources. The vocabulary:

- **Identities**: users, groups, and **service accounts / roles** representing apps.
- **Roles / policies**: sets of permissions.
- **Resource bindings**: attach permissions to specific resources.

### 2.1 GCP

- Cloud Functions / Cloud Run run under a **service account**. Give that account only the permissions it needs (least privilege), and do not use the default, over-privileged compute service account.
- If a function is not public, callers need the invoker permission (roles/run.invoker or the Cloud Functions equivalent).

### 2.2 AWS

- A Lambda has an **execution role** (what the function may do, for example write logs, read a secret, publish to a queue).
- A **resource-based policy** controls who may invoke it (for example allowing API Gateway to call it).
- Lambda does not assume a role automatically; you assign the execution role explicitly.

### 2.3 Principles

- **Least privilege** everywhere; a **dedicated identity per function/service**.
- Ensure every function can **write logs**, or debugging becomes very hard.
- Restrict who can invoke; do not expose functions publicly unless truly required.

## 3\. Why an API Gateway is mandatory

Both providers can expose a function directly, but in this project **all public entry points must go through an API Gateway** (or equivalent). The gateway gives you:

- **A single, stable endpoint** that you can version, route, and throttle without touching functions.
- **Authentication and authorization** at the edge (JWT, OAuth2, IAM, API keys, signature checks upstream of the function).
- **Rate limiting and throttling** to protect the backend from spikes and abuse.
- **Centralized logging and monitoring** of all incoming requests.
- **Request transformation and routing** before invoking the function.

## 4\. The proxy pattern (used throughout the project)

Public-facing functions are **thin proxies**: they authenticate the request, acknowledge quickly, and publish an event to a broker. The real work happens asynchronously in worker functions. This keeps latency low, decouples components, and absorbs bursts.

client -> API Gateway -> proxy fn (auth + validate + ack) -> broker (queue/topic) -> worker fn(s)

You will apply this to both the Discord interactions and the web frontend (see C06 and C07).

## 5\. A minimal secure function

Conceptually, a first HTTP function that you then place behind the gateway:

- 1\. Receive the request at the gateway.
- 2\. The gateway forwards to the function (function itself not publicly reachable).
- 3\. The function authenticates the caller (IAM, API key, or an upstream signature check).
- 4\. The function returns a small response quickly (and, in the real project, publishes an event).

Example call through the gateway once secured:

curl -H "Authorization: &lt;token&gt;" https://&lt;your-api-endpoint&gt;/hello

## 6. Security best practices

- Create a **dedicated service account / role per function**.
- Grant only the specific permissions needed (invoke, publish to a specific topic/queue, read a specific secret, write to a specific bucket/table).
- Store secrets (Discord bot token and public key, OAuth client secret, signing keys, etc) in the **secret manager**, and grant read access per function through IAM.
- Enforce **HTTPS**

## 7\. Checklist

- Deploy a simple function on your provider.
- Make it non-public and reachable only through an API Gateway.
- Give it a dedicated least-privilege identity that can write logs.
- Call it through the gateway with authentication.
- Read a value from the secret manager from the function using its IAM permissions.
- Commits are signed.

## 8\. Key takeaways

- Functions are stateless, event-triggered, auto-scaling, pay-per-use compute; keep them single-purpose.
- Secure them with least-privilege IAM permissions and a dedicated identity per function.
- Put every public entry point behind an API Gateway for auth, throttling, and monitoring.
- Use the proxy pattern: authenticate and acknowledge fast, then process asynchronously.
- Keep secrets in the secret manager and enforce HTTPS.

# C06 - Event-Driven Serverless Architecture & Data Design

_Reference material for the module_ **_Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless_**_. This support covers the architecture of the pixel-canvas application: event-driven design, message brokers, serverless storage, and the data model for a very large grid. It ends with_ **_Hands-on 3_**_: a first Discord-interaction function behind an API Gateway, validating auth and publishing an event, deployed through CI/CD._

## 1\. Goal and mandatory constraints

Design a cloud architecture that is scalable, maintainable, and strictly serverless. The binding constraints (from the subject):

- **100% serverless** for the application: no VMs, no Kubernetes workloads, no manual servers.
- **All public endpoints go through an API Gateway**; functions are never invokable directly over the internet.
- **Event-driven and asynchronous**: real work flows through a **message broker**. Only lightweight proxy functions acknowledge HTTP requests and publish events.
- **Single Responsibility Principle**: one function, one job.
- **Serverless persistence only**: serverless NoSQL and object storage. No SQL/managed DB.
- **Least privilege** IAM with a dedicated identity per function/service.
- **Everything deployed as Infrastructure as Code** through CI/CD (same GitFlow as the foundation).

## 2\. Serverless services to compose

Non-exhaustive; justify each choice at the defense.

- **GCP**: Cloud Run / Cloud Functions (compute), Pub/Sub or EventArc (messaging), Firestore (NoSQL), Cloud Storage (objects), API Gateway (edge), Secret Manager, Cloud Monitoring/Logging/Trace.
- **AWS**: Lambda (compute), SQS / SNS / EventBridge (messaging), DynamoDB (NoSQL), S3 (objects), API Gateway (edge), Secrets Manager, CloudWatch / X-Ray.

## 3\. Events and messaging

Event-driven design decouples producers from consumers, enabling scalability, resilience, and asynchronous processing.

### 3.1 Concepts

- **Event**: a record that something happened (a pixel draw was requested).
- **Producer / consumer**: emits / reacts to events.
- **Topic / queue**: the channel; **subscription**: delivery to a consumer.
- **Fan-out / fan-in**: one event triggers several consumers; several events are consolidated by one.

### 3.2 Brokers

- **GCP**: Pub/Sub (topics + subscriptions), EventArc (routes provider events such as Cloud Storage ObjectCreated or Firestore changes to functions).
- **AWS**: SQS (queues), SNS (pub/sub broadcast), EventBridge (event bus and routing), plus event sources like S3 events and DynamoDB Streams.

Two concrete examples of an event-driven serverless composition, one per provider:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### 3.3 Topic/queue design

Separate concerns into distinct channels, for example:

- pixel.draw -> draw requests
- discord.command -> commands issued by the bot
- snapshot.requested / snapshot.ready -> snapshot workflow

### 3.4 Reliability

- Configure **Dead Letter Queues / Topics** for failed messages so nothing is silently lost, and so retries are safe.
- Set **retention** long enough to process, replay, and debug.
- Design **idempotent** consumers: the same event may be delivered more than once or timestamp ordered.

## 4\. Serverless storage and the large grid

### 4.1 Object storage (buckets)

Ideal for binary/static content: snapshot images and the static frontend assets. Serverless, cheap, versioned, IAM-controlled. Never make application buckets public; serve snapshots through **signed (pre-authenticated) URLs**.

### 4.2 Serverless NoSQL

Firestore / DynamoDB hold the structured state: pixels, rate limits, and session flags. They scale automatically with low-latency key access and flexible schema.

### 4.3 Data model for a 10000x10000 (or infinite) grid

Storing the whole grid as a single document is not acceptable at this size. Design for performance and cost:

- **Chunk / tile** the grid (for example 64x64 or 256x256 tiles). Key by tile coordinates; store only painted pixels within a tile.
- Record, per pixel of the current state, at least **color**, **author**, and **update timestamp** so a user can inspect any pixel.
- Consider **delta / event-based** updates: transmit only changed pixels to the frontend.
- Consider **periodic snapshots** (full image) plus edits since the last snapshot for fast recovery and initial load.
- Use **caching** (CDN, in-memory) with proper invalidation for frequent reads.
- Enforce **per-user rate limiting** (default for example 20 pixels/minute, overridable by the admin command) and maintain **consistency under concurrent writes** (atomic updates/transactions where needed).

### 4.4 Choosing storage

| **Use case**                       | **Storage**          | **Reason**                     |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Snapshot images, static assets     | Bucket (GCS/S3)      | Cheap, scalable, file-oriented |
| ---                                | ---                  | ---                            |
| Pixel state, rate limits, sessions | Firestore / DynamoDB | Low-latency structured access  |
| ---                                | ---                  | ---                            |
| Real-time distribution             | Broker + change feed | Only push changed pixels       |
| ---                                | ---                  | ---                            |

## 5\. Discord interactions: how the entry point works

Discord sends **interactions** (slash commands) as HTTPS POSTs to your configured endpoint (your API Gateway). Your proxy must:

- 1\. **Verify the signature** using your Discord application&apos;s public key (Ed25519), reading the X-Signature-Ed25519 and X-Signature-Timestamp headers over the raw body. Reject invalid signatures with 401.
- 2\. Respond to the **PING** (type: 1) with a **PONG** (type: 1).
- 3\. For commands, **acknowledge fast**: return a deferred response (type: 5) and publish a discord.command event; a worker performs the action and edits the response or posts a follow-up.

This keeps the bot serverless and within Discord&apos;s 3-second response budget.

## 6\. Architecture diagram expectations

Your diagram is part of the defense and must match reality. Make it **provider-specific** (use the official GCP/AWS icon sets), and show:

- Entry points (API Gateway), proxies, workers, brokers, NoSQL, buckets.
- **Request flow** (client -> gateway -> proxy -> broker) and **event flow** (broker -> workers -> storage -> real-time channel).
- **IAM boundaries** and protocols on the arrows.
- The **real-time path** back to the frontend.

Keep the layers clear and one-directional for requests: user interactions (Discord / web) -> gateway -> proxies -> broker -> workers -> data.

Keep it maintained as the implementation evolves. Recommended tools: Draw.io, Lucidchart, Cloudcraft, or the Google Cloud architecture tool.

## 7\. Reference

The subject and this support use a precise vocabulary. When a word appears in a requirement, it carries an expectation. This section is the reference for what each term means in the context of your project, and what we expect to see behind it at the defense.

**Entry point.** The single place where traffic from the outside world enters your system. In this project the entry point is an **API Gateway**. Expectation: nothing else is publicly reachable. Functions are invoked by the gateway or by events, never called directly from the internet.

**Proxy.** A thin function placed right behind the gateway whose only responsibility is to receive a request, check it, and hand it off. Expectation: it validates and forwards; it does not do the heavy work, does not write the grid, and does not block. It authenticates or verifies the request, publishes an event, and returns immediately.

**Event.** A record that something happened (for example, a pixel draw was requested). Expectation: events are the unit of internal communication. Work is triggered by events, not by one function directly calling another and waiting for the answer.

**Event-driven / asynchronous.** A design where a producer emits an event and moves on, and a consumer reacts to it later, independently. Expectation: the request path returns to the user quickly (acknowledge now, process later). Real work happens off the critical path.

**Broker.** The channel that carries events between producers and consumers, implemented as a **queue** or a **topic**. Expectation: a broker sits between your proxies and your workers so the two are decoupled. It absorbs bursts, smooths load, and is the reason the system can scale and stay resilient. Concerns are separated into distinct channels, with proper retention and retry configuration.

**Publish / consume.** To publish is to put an event on the broker; to consume is to read and process it. Expectation: proxies publish, workers consume. A worker that consumes an event owns the processing of that event.

**Worker.** A function that consumes events from the broker and performs the actual business logic (rate limiting, writing a pixel, rendering a snapshot). Expectation: workers are where the real work lives, and they run independently of the request that triggered them.

**Idempotent.** Processing the same event more than once produces the same result as processing it once. Expectation: because brokers can deliver a message more than once, your workers must tolerate duplicates without corrupting the grid or double-counting.

**Retry and dead-letter queue (DLQ).** A retry re-delivers an event that failed to process; a dead-letter queue collects events that keep failing after several attempts. Expectation: transient failures are retried automatically, and poison messages end up in a DLQ instead of blocking the pipeline or being lost silently.

**Real-time updates.** Changes to the grid reaching the web frontend live, without the user polling. Expectation: this is driven from the data layer, either by fanning out a "pixel processed" event to a real-time channel, or by streaming changes from the NoSQL **change feed** (depending on your infrastructure, these events may be produced automatically by your storage).

**Change feed / streaming.** A stream of the changes happening in a data store that other components can subscribe to. Expectation: used to push only the pixels that actually changed, rather than re-sending the whole grid.

**Snapshot.** A rendered image of the current grid at a point in time. Expectation: a snapshot is generated on demand or scheduled, stored in a bucket, and shared through a link, not streamed inline.

**Signed (pre-authenticated) URL.** A time-limited URL that grants access to a specific object in storage without making the bucket public. Expectation: snapshots are returned to Discord as signed URLs; the bucket itself stays private.

**Fan-out.** One event triggered several independent consumers. Expectation: use it where a single change must reach multiple places.

## 8\. Hands-on 3: first Discord-interaction function

**Goal**: a Discord slash command reaches a function through your API Gateway; the function validates the signature, acknowledges, and publishes an event to a queue/topic. Everything is deployed by Terraform through a CI/CD pipeline.

### Steps

1. 1\. **Register a Discord application** and one slash command (for example /draw). Note the application **public key** and **bot token**; store them in the **secret manager** (never in the repo).
2. 2\. **Provision, as Terraform**: the function (proxy), the API Gateway route to it, the broker topic/queue (for example discord.command), and a **least-privilege identity** for the function (read the Discord public key secret, publish to that one topic/queue, write logs).
3. 3\. **Implement the proxy** so it: verifies the Ed25519 signature over the raw request body, replies to PING with PONG, for /draw, returns a deferred acknowledgement and publishes an event with the parsed parameters and a generated correlation_id.
4. 4\. **Set Discord interaction endpoint URL** to your API Gateway URL and confirm Discord&apos;s validation succeeds (it sends a signed PING).
5. 5\. **Deploy through CI/CD**: a PR runs validate/plan; a release tag applies to dev (and prd) using OIDC. No manual deploys.
6. 6\. **Verify**: invoke /draw in Discord, confirm the acknowledgement, and confirm a message landed on the topic/queue (check the console or a temporary logging subscriber).

**Acceptance**: the command travels client -> API Gateway -> proxy -> broker; the signature is validated (invalid signatures rejected); secrets come from the secret manager; the function is not publicly invokable outside the gateway; the whole thing was deployed by the pipeline.

**Go further**: add the command-worker that consumes discord.command.

## 9\. Key takeaways

- The application is strictly serverless, event-driven, and deployed as IaC through CI/CD.
- Proxies authenticate and acknowledge; brokers decouple; workers do one job each.
- Use buckets for images/assets and serverless NoSQL for state; never expose buckets publicly.
- Design the grid with chunking, deltas, snapshots, and caching for large-scale performance.
- Validate Discord signatures and acknowledge within the time budget.

# C07 - Discord Bot, Real-Time Frontend & Snapshots

_Reference material for the module_ **_Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless_**_. This support details the application surface: the mandatory Discord commands, the real-time serverless frontend with a brush tool, the snapshot workflow, and Discord OAuth2. All of it runs on the event-driven, serverless architecture from C06._

## 1\. Discord bot (serverless, interactions only)

The bot uses **Discord Interactions** (slash commands) with the interaction endpoint pointing at **your API Gateway**. Using a persistent gateway SDK (discord.js, discord.py in a long-running process) is **off subject**: it is not serverless.

Recap of the request path (from C06): every command goes **API Gateway -> proxy fn (verify signature + acknowledge) -> broker -> worker fn**.

### 1.1 Mandatory commands

Implement exactly these. Naming can be kept; behavior and parameters are fixed.

<div class="joplin-table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th><p><strong>Command</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Parameters</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Behavior</strong></p></th><th><p><strong>Authz</strong></p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/draw</code></pre></th><th><p>x (int), y (int), color</p></th><th><p>Draw one pixel at (x, y) with color. Rate-limited per user. Acknowledge immediately, process async.</p></th><th><p>any user</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/get</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Return the current grid as a PNG/JPEG image.</p></th><th><p>any user</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/snapshot</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Generate a timestamped PNG/JPEG, store it in a bucket, return a signed URL in the channel.</p></th><th><p>admin</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/admin pause</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Pause drawing globally (draws rejected while paused).</p></th><th><p>admin</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/admin resume</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Resume drawing.</p></th><th><p>admin</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/admin clear</code></pre></th><th><p>none</p></th><th><p>Clear the entire grid.</p></th><th><p>admin</p></th></tr><tr><th><pre><code>/admin ratelimit</code></pre></th><th><p>user, limit (int/min)</p></th><th><p>Set a per-user rate-limit override.</p></th><th><p>admin</p></th></tr></thead></table></div>

Rules:

- **Admin authorization** must be enforced (a Discord role or an allow-list you control). A normal user must not be able to run admin commands.
- Every command is **asynchronous**: the proxy returns a deferred acknowledgement (type: 5), the worker performs the action and edits the response or posts a follow-up.
- /draw respects the current pause state and the user&apos;s rate limit.

### 1.2 Command worker responsibilities

- **draw**: validate, check pause + rate limit, write the pixel (color, author, timestamp), emit pixel.processed.
- **get**: render the current visible canvas to an image and return it.
- **snapshot**: emit snapshot.requested (the snapshot workflow handles the rest).
- **admin.\***: verify admin authorization, then update session state (pause flag, clear the grid) or the rate-limit override.

## 2\. Snapshot workflow

/snapshot -> command-worker emits snapshot.requested

```
snapshot-worker: read current grid -> compose PNG/JPEG (timestamped) -> put in bucket
bucket ObjectCreated == snapshot.ready
notifier fn: generate a signed (pre-authenticated) URL -> post it to the Discord channel
```

- The bucket is **not public**; access is granted through **signed URLs** with a limited lifetime.
- The image name/metadata carries a **timestamp**.
- Keep the workflow event-driven (the bucket event triggers the notifier), not a synchronous chain.

## 3\. Real-time serverless frontend

### 3.1 Hosting

Any **serverless** hosting/technology of your choice: static hosting + CDN, Cloud Run, App Engine, CloudFront + Lambda@Edge, or a Discord Activity. No self-managed backend or VM.

### 3.2 Authentication (Discord OAuth2)

Users log in with **Discord OAuth2** (or custom identities linked to their Discord account).

Flow:

- 1\. User clicks &quot;Login with Discord&quot;; redirect to Discord with your client id, the identify scope, and your redirect URI.
- 2\. User consents; Discord redirects back with an authorization code.
- 3\. Exchange the code for an access token, read the Discord user id, link it to your system.
- 4\. The user acts on the canvas with their linked identity.

**Good practices**: keep scopes minimal (identify is enough), always use HTTPS, validate redirect URIs, and do **not** persist the user&apos;s Discord access token server-side.

### 3.3 Real-time updates (no polling)

This is a hard requirement: the canvas must update through **events / streaming**. **Polling and manual refresh buttons are not allowed**, and the displayed state must be the up-to-date state at any moment.

Implement a real-time channel that pushes only **changed pixels**, for example:

- Firestore real-time listeners (GCP),
- WebSocket API (AWS API Gateway WebSocket) or server-sent events fronting a broker subscription,
- a managed pub/sub-to-client bridge.

The frontend subscribes and applies deltas as they arrive. A pixel drawn via Discord must appear on the web canvas without a manual refresh or using polling, and vice versa.

### 3.4 Performance on a 10000x10000 (or infinite) grid

The frontend must stay responsive at full scale:

- Render only the **visible viewport**; support **zoom and pan**.
- **Load chunks/tiles** on demand rather than the whole grid.
- Apply **incremental deltas** from the real-time channel; avoid full reloads.
- Use canvas/WebGL rendering rather than DOM elements per pixel.
- Cache immutable tiles; invalidate on change.

### 3.5 Pixel inspection

A user must be able to **select a pixel** and see its **author** and **update timestamp**, and to draw on it.

### 3.6 Brush tool (required)

Provide a **brush** that draws **multiple pixels at once**, with a **configurable brush size**. A brush stroke should produce the affected pixels and send them through the same authenticated gateway + event pipeline (batch the changed pixels into events; do not write directly to storage from the client). Respect pause state and rate limits.

This feature will help you to demonstrate your drawing scaling capabilities.

## 4\. Everything through the pipeline

- All frontend API calls are **authenticated** and go through the **API Gateway -> proxy -> broker** path. No direct writes to storage from the browser.
- The bot, the workers, the frontend, and their infrastructure are deployed as **Infrastructure as Code** through **CI/CD** with the same GitFlow as the foundation.
- Secrets live in the **secret manager**; functions read them through least-privilege IAM.

## 5\. Common pitfalls (seen in past defenses)

- Polling or a refresh button instead of real-time updates (penalized).
- Public functions or public buckets; buckets used as a database.
- Direct client writes bypassing the gateway/queue.
- One giant grid document that does not scale.
- Missing admin authorization checks in the worker.
- Secrets hardcoded, or over-privileged default service accounts.
- Diagrams that do not match the real implementation.

## 6\. Checklist

- All mandatory Discord commands are implemented and asynchronous.
- Admin authorization enforced in the worker.
- Snapshot stored in a non-public bucket and shared via signed URL.
- Frontend on serverless hosting, Discord OAuth2 login, minimal scopes.
- Real-time updates with no polling; the webapp is always in sync.
- Performant on the full 10000x10000 grid (viewport, tiles, deltas).
- Pixel selection shows author and timestamp.
- Brush tool with configurable size, batched through the pipeline.
- Deployed by IaC + CI/CD; secrets from the secret manager.
- Commits are signed.

## 7\. Key takeaways

- The bot is interactions-only and serverless; all commands are predefined and asynchronous.
- Snapshots flow through a bucket event to a notifier that returns a signed URL.
- The frontend is serverless, authenticated with Discord OAuth2, and updates in real time.
- Large-grid performance comes from viewport rendering, tiling, deltas, and caching.
- The brush draws many pixels at once through the same authenticated event pipeline.

# C08 - Monitoring, Logging, Tracing & Alerting

Reference material for the module **Cloud Native: DevOps, IaC & Serverless**. This support covers observability for the whole system: the cluster hosting your runners and the serverless application. You choose the tools; you must meet the requirements.

## 1\. Why observability is not optional

You are operating two very different layers (a Kubernetes cluster and an event-driven serverless app) that must behave under load. Without observability you cannot detect issues early, understand performance, prove scalability, or debug a distributed flow. In past defenses, missing traces, dashboards, and alerts were among the most common reasons strong projects lost points.

Observability rests on three pillars:

- **Metrics**: quantitative time series (CPU, memory, node/pod counts, invocations, errors, latency, queue depth).
- **Logs**: event records (draws, commands, errors, state changes).
- **Traces**: the path of a single request across services.

Your solution must cover all three for both layers.

## 2\. Requirements

You must be able to:

1. **1\. See cluster metrics and state**: CPU, RAM, node count, pod count, and self-hosted runner activity.
2. **2\. See serverless application metrics and state**: invocations, errors, latency, queue depth / message age, DLQ counts.
3. **3\. Integrate application logs and traces** into your monitoring solution and be able to **search and analyze** them, and to **trace a single request end to end** using a **correlation id** (or similar) propagated across services.
4. **4\. Set up alerts** for critical issues (high error rate, high latency, queue backlog, resource saturation).

And you must be able to **demonstrate scalability** during the defense: show, through your monitoring, that the system scales and stays performant under load. A load test (script or a tool such as Locust) is one option; the brush drawing many pixels at once can also generate the load. What matters is proving it, not the method.

## 3\. Tooling options

You are free to choose, as long as you meet the requirements and can justify your choices. Common building blocks:

- **Prometheus**: metrics collection and storage, PromQL queries. Deployable with Helm; on managed clusters you can also use the managed Prometheus services (Google Managed Service for Prometheus, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus).
- **Grafana**: dashboards and alerting over Prometheus, cloud monitoring, and traces.
- **OpenTelemetry (OTel)**: vendor-neutral SDKs and a collector for traces, metrics, and logs, exporting to Prometheus/Grafana or to cloud backends.
- **Cloud-native services**: Cloud Monitoring / Cloud Logging / Cloud Trace (GCP), or CloudWatch / X-Ray (AWS). These integrate naturally with serverless and require no cluster to run.

A pragmatic split for this project: use **cloud-native monitoring** for the serverless app (it is the path of least resistance and integrates with the managed services), and either managed Prometheus + Grafana or the cloud monitoring for the **cluster/runners**. Whatever you choose, deploy it as code where applicable and justify it.

## 4\. Monitoring the cluster and runners

- Expose node and pod metrics (a node exporter / the cluster&apos;s metrics pipeline) and scrape them (Prometheus) or use the managed metrics.
- Track: node count, CPU/memory per node, pod count, and **runner activity** (jobs running, queue of pending jobs, scale up/down events).
- Build a dashboard that makes **node autoscaling visible**: when runner demand rises, you should see nodes being added, and removed when idle. This is exactly what you will show at the defense to prove foundation scalability.

For the dashboard itself you have multiples valid options: run your own **Grafana**, **Kibana**, etc and hosting it in the cluster on top of Prometheus (ideally managed by your cloud provider), or use the **managed monitoring solution offered by your cloud provider** (Cloud Monitoring on GCP, CloudWatch, dashboards on AWS). Either is accepted; pick one and justify it.

An example of dashboard with grafana:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## 5\. Monitoring the serverless application

Track the health of the event-driven pipeline:

- **Function metrics**: invocations, errors, duration/latency, concurrency, throttles.
- **Queue/topic metrics**: depth (pending messages), **message age** (how long a message waits), processing latency, and **DLQ entries** (failed messages).
- **Storage**: read/write patterns and errors on NoSQL and buckets.

Queues are the heart of the system; a growing backlog or a filling DLQ is your earliest signal of trouble.

## 6\. Logging and tracing with a correlation id (or similar)

- Emit **structured (JSON) logs** with consistent fields: correlation_id, trace_id, user_id, the function name, and the event type.
- Generate a **correlation id** (or similar) at the first entry point (the proxy) and **propagate** it on the event through every worker, so a single Discord command or web draw can be followed end to end.
- Instrument functions for **tracing**:
  - AWS: X-Ray (SDK or OpenTelemetry), capturing downstream calls.
  - GCP: Cloud Trace via OpenTelemetry.
- Ensure every function&apos;s identity has permission to **write logs and traces**, or you will be blind.

Conceptual structured log entry:

{

```
 "function": "draw-worker",
 "message": "pixel processed",
 "correlation_id": "abc-123",
 "trace_id": "...",
 "user_id": "1234",
 "x": 10, "y": 20, "color": "#ff0000"
}
```

## 7\. Alerting

Monitoring without alerting is logging that no one reads. Define alerts on meaningful conditions and route them somewhere you will see (email, chat webhook, discord messages, etc.). Examples:

- Function **error rate** above a threshold, or a spike in throttles.
- **Latency** above a target (proxy acknowledgement time, worker processing time).
- **Queue backlog**: message age or depth above a threshold, or **DLQ count > 0**.
- **Cluster saturation**: node/pod pressure, or runner jobs stuck pending too long.

You must have at least one meaningful alert on a resource metric and one on an application-level issue.

## 8\. Demonstrating scalability (defense)

Be ready to generate load and show, through your monitoring, that the system scales and stays performant under load. The method is up to you (a load test such as a script or Locust, or simply the brush drawing many pixels at once); the monitoring is what proves it.

- For the **foundation**: drive enough CI/CD or synthetic runner load to trigger **node autoscaling**, and show it on your dashboard.
- For the **application**: generate a burst of draw events (brush, a script hitting the gateway, etc) and show functions scaling and the queue buffering and draining, with latency and error rates staying healthy.

Scaling cannot be assumed; it must be tested and observable on your monitoring.

## 9\. Checklist

- Cluster dashboard: nodes, pods, CPU/RAM, runner activity, autoscaling visible.
- App dashboard: invocations, errors, latency, queue depth/age, DLQ.
- Structured logs with a correlation id propagated across services.
- Traces for the end-to-end path of one request.
- At least one resource alert and one application alert, routed to a real channel.
- A way to generate load to demonstrate foundation and application scaling on your monitoring.
